intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of all publicly trusted certificates, with ISRG leading at 32% share, followed by Google Trust Services at 21% and DigiCert at 18%. Market concentration measured by HHI stands at 1981, indicating a moderately concentrated market where a handful of players dominate while 74 tail CAs collectively issue the remaining volume. This structure creates systemic dependencies where operational failures at top providers would immediately affect a third of the encrypted web.
intros.trust: 335 root certificates are distributed across the four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores and only 38 CA owners achieve universal presence. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating a fragmented trust landscape where certificate chains validated by Edge may fail in other browsers. This disagreement forces CAs to maintain multiple certificate paths and complicates incident response, as distrust decisions by one program may not affect sites viewed through Microsoft browsers.
intros.conc: The top three CAs issue 71% of all certificates and the HHI of 1981 signals moderate concentration with systemic risk concentrated in fewer than five organizations. ISRG's 32% share means nearly one-third of the encrypted web depends on a single nonprofit's operational continuity. When combined with the 88 total trusted CAs, the market shows a bifurcated structure where a small oligopoly serves the vast majority of the web while a long tail of 74 CAs holds the same root store privileges despite minimal market presence.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate with full trust store inclusion while collectively representing the minority of issuance volume, creating asymmetric risk where low-volume operators face identical compliance requirements as major providers. These tail CAs contribute disproportionately to governance overhead, generating incidents that require root program review despite serving small constituencies. The combination of full trust privileges and minimal operational scale means a single compromised tail CA can issue certificates for any domain on the internet while serving fewer than 0.1% of actual users.
intros.geo: US-incorporated CAs issue 93% of all publicly trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of the 88 trusted authorities, while 44 European CAs collectively hold 7% share and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs account for 0.09%. This geographic concentration means American corporate governance, bankruptcy law, and regulatory jurisdiction effectively control the global certificate infrastructure. The gap between CA count and issuance share reveals that most non-US CAs operate as trusted but minimally-used tail providers, holding global privileges while serving regional or niche markets.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold positions in global trust stores but collectively issue only 0.09% of certificates, concentrated primarily in Asia-Pacific jurisdictions. These CAs possess technical capability to issue certificates for any domain despite minimal legitimate market presence, creating a trust surface that extends far beyond their operational footprint. The presence of state-controlled CAs in root programs represents a persistent governance challenge where geopolitical considerations intersect with technical trust decisions.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high legal risk due to frameworks enabling compelled access or undermining of cryptographic systems: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk where legal ambiguity or surveillance frameworks could compel CA cooperation without public disclosure. These classifications affect 7 of the 30 government CAs and multiple commercial providers operating under these legal regimes, creating scenarios where lawful orders could force certificate misissuance without triggering breach disclosure requirements.
intros.ops: 1,716 total compliance incidents have been recorded across 55 CAs, with misissuance leading at 658 cases, followed by 555 governance failures and 372 revocation issues. CAs self-report only 30% of their own incidents, while external researchers discover 17%, automated tools find 15%, and formal audits catch just 7%, revealing a systemic detection gap. Of the 1,716 incidents, 230 represent explicit policy failures, 157 involve disclosure failures, and 110 were audit findings, demonstrating that even third-party oversight misses the majority of compliance breakdowns.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has largely converged on RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-384 algorithms, with legacy SHA-1 roots remaining in trust stores only to validate old intermediate certificates under technical constraints. Active issuance relies exclusively on SHA-256 or stronger digest algorithms as required by baseline standards. The transition to post-quantum cryptography represents the next major shift, though current root programs have not yet mandated migration timelines or algorithm suites.
intros.distrust: 16 browser distrust events have been recorded, with 14 triggered by compliance or operational failures and 10 involving patterns of repeated issues rather than isolated incidents. Root program analysis classified CA posture as negligent noncompliance in 7 cases, demonstrated incompetence in 3, and willful circumvention in 3, showing that distrust typically follows sustained dysfunction rather than single mistakes. The median runway from distrust announcement to final removal is 1,185 days, giving relying parties over three years to migrate but also extending the period where distrusted CAs remain active in some contexts.
intros.policy: Of 35 active TLS-issuing CAs measured, only 8 already issue certificates meeting the 47-day validity threshold planned for March 2029, while 5 remain at risk of noncompliance with the 100-day limit coming in March 2027. The median CA currently issues 62-day certificates, above the intermediate March 2027 threshold but requiring operational changes before the final step. Readiness is complicated by the regulatory surface CAs must navigate, which has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total requirements, of which 76% are mandatory, distributed across CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF/ISO/NIST standards.
intros.governance: Chrome provided substantive oversight comments on 18% of the 223 compliance incidents in 2025, down from 68% coverage in 2019, while Mozilla dropped from 78% to 10% and Apple covered just 5%. Microsoft provided zero substantive comments in 2025 despite operating a root program with 142 unique roots. This declining oversight trend concentrates governance burden on Chrome's 115 recent substantive comments while reducing accountability for the 82% of incidents that receive no public root program engagement.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 contribute actively to ballot development, leaving 35 with zero contribution to the standards they must implement. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots, demonstrating concentrated policy leadership within a small group of participants. This participation gap means a minority of CAs shape requirements binding on all 88 trusted authorities, while the silent majority implements standards without contributing to their design.
intros.audit: Auditors caught 31% of the 429 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, meaning 69% of compliance failures coexisted with clean audit opinions. 42 CAs show high transparency gaps where incident histories diverge sharply from audit letters, 6 CAs received qualified opinions noting control deficiencies, and only 12 CAs have transitioned to ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5 despite its availability since 2025. WebTrust CAs self-report compliance gaps in 63% of letters and ETSI CAs in 70%, but this self-disclosure appears disconnected from the 1,716 incidents recorded in public bug trackers, revealing a systemic surveillance gap where annual audits function more as attestation theater than operational assurance.
